def: Elementary transformations are simple operations on rows or columns of a matrix (swap, scale, add a multiple of one row to another) that simplify the matrix without changing the solution of the underlying system.
points: Ri <-> Rj means swap row i and row j.
Ri -> kRi means multiply row i by a nonzero constant k.
Ri -> Ri + kRj means add k times row j to row i.
Use these to convert a matrix step by step into identity form or echelon form.
The same operations can be done on columns instead of rows.
Do only one operation per step and write it clearly for full marks.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Original matrix"] --> B["Apply row operation"]
  B --> C["Simplified matrix"]
  C --> D["Repeat until goal reached"]

example: Matrix [[2,4],[1,3]]: apply R1 -> R1 - 2R2 to get [[0,-2],[1,3]], simplifying the first row.
tip: Write the operation name (like R1 -> R1 - 2R2) before every step — examiners check this working.

def: The inverse of a matrix A is found as A^-1 = (1/det A) times adj A, where adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix of A.
points: First find det A; if det A = 0, inverse does not exist.
Find the cofactor of every element (minor with sign (-1)^(i+j)).
Arrange cofactors into the cofactor matrix.
Take the transpose of the cofactor matrix to get adj A.
Multiply adj A by 1/det A to get A^-1.
Always verify A * A^-1 = I if time permits.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Matrix A"] --> B["Find det A"]
  A --> C["Find cofactors"]
  C --> D["Transpose to get adj A"]
  B --> E["A inverse = adj A / det A"]
  D --> E

tip: Show the cofactor matrix step separately before writing adj A — it is a scoring step on its own.

def: This method finds A^-1 by writing [A | I] side by side and applying row operations until the left block becomes I; the right block then becomes A^-1.
points: Write the matrix A next to the identity matrix I of the same size.
Apply the same row operation to both sides at every step.
Aim to make the diagonal entries 1 and off-diagonal entries 0 on the left.
Once left block is I, the right block gives A^-1.
If you cannot reduce the left side to I, A is not invertible.
This method avoids computing determinants and cofactors.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Write A beside I"] --> B["Apply row operations to both sides"]
  B --> C["Left side becomes I"]
  C --> D["Right side is A inverse"]

tip: Write every row operation used in each step on the side — missing steps loses process marks even if the final answer is right.

t: Solving linear equations by matrix method
def: A system of linear equations can be written as AX = B, and solved by X = A^-1 B once A^-1 is known.
points: Write the equations in the form AX = B, listing coefficients in A, variables in X, constants in B.
Check det A is not zero, so A^-1 exists.
Find A^-1 by adjoint or elementary transformation method.
Multiply A^-1 by B to get X.
The entries of X give the values of the variables directly.
Verify by substituting values back into original equations.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Write as AX = B"] --> B["Find A inverse"]
  B --> C["Compute X = A inverse times B"]
  C --> D["Read x, y, z values"]

tip: State A, X, B clearly at the start — examiners award a mark just for correct setup.

def: The echelon (reduction) method solves a system by reducing the augmented matrix [A | B] with row operations until the equations become simple enough for back-substitution.
points: Write the augmented matrix [A | B] with coefficients and constants together.
Use row operations to make zeros below the leading entries (echelon form).
The bottom rows now give simple equations in fewer variables.
Solve the simplest equation first, then substitute upward (back-substitution).
If a row reduces to 0 = nonzero, the system has no solution.
If a row reduces to 0 = 0, the system has infinitely many solutions.
formula: [A | B] -> row reduce -> echelon form -> back-substitute

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Augmented matrix A given B"] --> B["Row reduce to echelon form"]
  B --> C["Solve last variable"]
  C --> D["Back substitute upward"]
  D --> E["Get all variable values"]

example: x+y+z=6, y+2z=5, z=2 (after reduction): from z=2, y=5-4=1, then x=6-1-2=3. Solution x=3,y=1,z=2.
tip: Clearly box or underline the echelon form before back-substituting, examiners look for this intermediate step.

def: These are standard rules satisfied by matrix inverses that simplify computation without redoing full inverse calculations.
points: A^-1 exists only when det A is not equal to zero (A is non-singular).
(A^-1)^-1 = A, the inverse of an inverse gives back the original matrix.
(AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1, note the reversed order.
(A^T)^-1 = (A^-1)^T, inverse and transpose commute.
det(A^-1) = 1/det A.
Identity matrix I is its own inverse: I^-1 = I.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["A exists inverse if det A not 0"] --> B["AB inverse equals B inverse times A inverse"]
  B --> C["Order reverses"]

example: If A and B are invertible 2x2 matrices, to find (AB)^-1 you compute B^-1 A^-1, not A^-1 B^-1.
tip: Quote the exact property name when asked a theory question — half the marks come from stating it correctly.
